title: Activity Selection — Maximizing Non-Overlapping Intervals
summary: The canonical greedy problem: pick the maximum number of non-overlapping activities by always taking the one that finishes earliest.

slides.markdown:
Given a set of activities, each with a start and finish time, choose the **largest possible subset** where no two chosen activities overlap. This is the reference greedy problem — the one nearly every textbook and interview guide uses to introduce the technique, because its correctness proof is clean and its greedy rule is genuinely surprising the first time you see it.

The rule: **sort by finish time, always take the next activity that starts after the last one you took ends.** Not by start time, not by duration — finish time specifically, for a reason this topic makes concrete.

slides.sectionTitle: Why finish time is the correct key
slides.markdown:
Sorting by finish time and always taking the earliest-finishing compatible activity leaves the **maximum possible remaining time** for everything after it, no matter how long that activity itself took or when it started.

This is the intuition behind the correctness proof (formalized fully in `exchange-argument`): whatever activity an optimal solution picks first, swapping in the earliest-finishing activity instead can never hurt — it frees up at least as much room for subsequent choices. Sorting by start time or duration doesn't have this property: an activity that starts earliest might run very long and block out many other activities; an activity that's shortest might still start so late it can't be combined with much else.

After sorting by finish time, scan once with a pointer tracking the finish time of the last accepted activity. Each new activity is accepted if its start time is >= that pointer, then the pointer updates to the new activity's finish time; otherwise it's skipped entirely.

![Six intervals sorted by finish time, with accepted intervals in one color and intervals skipped for starting too early in another](assets/activity-selection-timeline.svg)

The scan never looks backward and never reconsiders a skipped activity — accept, skip, accept, in one linear pass.

assets.alt: Six intervals sorted by finish time, with accepted intervals in one color and intervals skipped for starting too early in another

slides.markdown:
```python
def activity_selection(activities):
    activities.sort(key=lambda a: a[1])  # sort by finish time
    count = 0
    last_finish = float('-inf')
    for start, finish in activities:
        if start >= last_finish:
            count += 1
            last_finish = finish
    return count
```

The entire algorithm is a sort plus one linear scan with a single running variable — no table, no backtracking, no revisiting a decision once made. This simplicity is exactly what a correct greedy buys you over the DP-style search a less-structured version of the same question might otherwise require.

Sorting by **start time** and greedily taking the earliest-starting compatible activity fails: the earliest-starting activity might run for a very long time, blocking out several short, later-starting activities that together would have been a larger set.

Sorting by **duration** (shortest first) also fails: a very short activity might still occupy an awkward slot that blocks two other activities on either side, when a differently-timed choice would have let both through. Only finish time gives the "frees up maximum remaining room" guarantee this problem needs — the other two orderings are intuitive-sounding but don't carry that guarantee, and constructing a small counterexample for each is a good exercise to actually internalize why.

| | Activity Selection | Meeting Rooms II |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Largest set of non-overlapping activities from ONE set | Minimum concurrent rooms to host ALL given meetings |
| Technique | Sort by finish time, greedily accept | Track concurrent overlap (two-pointer sweep or min-heap) |
| What's being optimized | Count of activities kept | Peak simultaneous demand |

These look similar ("intervals," "overlap") but ask fundamentally different questions: Activity Selection *discards* some activities to keep as many non-overlapping ones as possible; Meeting Rooms II must accommodate *every* meeting and asks how much concurrent capacity that requires. Conflating the two produces code that solves the wrong problem — `meeting-rooms`, in the `intervals` group, covers the second one in full.

O(n log n), driven entirely by the sort. The scan itself is a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra state (just the last-accepted finish time). If the activities arrive pre-sorted by finish time — which some problem variants guarantee — the whole algorithm drops to O(n).

This is worth stating explicitly in an interview: naming that the sort is the bottleneck, and that a pre-sorted input would change the complexity, signals you understand where the cost actually comes from rather than treating "O(n log n)" as a fixed label for the whole problem.

Does an activity ending at time 5 conflict with one starting at time 5? The answer depends entirely on the problem's own definition, and getting it backward silently changes the answer by one activity in either direction.

Most activity-selection formulations treat `start >= last_finish` (not `>`) as compatible — an activity can begin the instant the previous one ends, since real-world scheduling usually allows back-to-back bookings. But some problem variants (particularly ones phrased around closed intervals `[start, end]` rather than half-open ones) require strict separation. Read the problem statement's exact wording on this before coding — don't assume either convention, and test the boundary case explicitly once you've picked one.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this is the reference greedy problem
slides.markdown:
Activity Selection earns its place as the canonical example because its correctness proof is unusually clean: the exchange argument for "finish time is safe" needs almost no extra machinery beyond "a compatible activity that ends no later than another compatible activity can always be swapped in without losing anything."

Many other greedy problems' proofs are less immediately obvious (Huffman coding's exchange argument, for instance, needs an extra step about tree depth). Treat this problem as the template: once you can reproduce its proof from memory, you have the pattern for approaching a new greedy problem's proof, even if the details differ. `exchange-argument`, next in this group, works through this exact proof formally.

**Weighted** activity selection — each activity has a value, and you maximize total value rather than count — breaks the greedy approach entirely, even though it looks like a small variation. A high-value activity that overlaps with several lower-value ones might still be worth choosing over all of them combined, and "finishes earliest" says nothing about value.

This variant needs DP: sort by finish time (still useful for defining a valid state order), then `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], value[i] + dp[last compatible activity before i])` — structurally identical to `dp-1d-sequences`' House Robber shape, just with a compatibility lookup instead of a fixed `i-2`. Recognizing when adding one axis (value) turns a clean greedy problem back into a DP one is exactly the judgment `greedy-vs-dp`, later in this group, builds explicitly.

If you need the actual list of chosen activities, not just the count, no extra bookkeeping is needed beyond what the scan already does — simply append each accepted activity to a result list at the moment it's accepted, since the greedy decision is final the instant it's made.

This is notably simpler than the reconstruction techniques needed in DP (`knapsack`'s backward walk, LIS's `prev` pointers): because greedy never revisits a choice, there's no need to walk anything backward afterward — the forward scan *is* the reconstruction. That simplicity is one more concrete payoff of a correctly-proven greedy algorithm over its DP counterpart.
